overview:
In Jain traditions, marriage (*vivāha*) is understood as a worldly, householder institution rather than a sacramental rite leading to spiritual liberation. Across Digambara and Śvetāmbara communities, marriage is framed within the broader ethics of *gṛhastha-dharma*—the duties of laypeople who pursue spiritual progress while remaining engaged in social life. Jain texts consistently emphasize that liberation (*mokṣa*) is attained through personal discipline, nonviolence, and detachment, not through marital status.

Marriage is treated as a voluntary social arrangement that supports stability, mutual responsibility, and ethical living. It is not a religious obligation, nor is it a prerequisite for spiritual advancement. The *Ācārāṅga Sūtra* and *Sūtrakṛtāṅga* describe the conduct of monks and nuns, who renounce marriage entirely, while lay conduct texts such as the *Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra* outline ethical expectations for householders, including fidelity, restraint, and non-harm within family life.

Historically, Jain communities developed distinct marriage customs—such as the *lagna-patrikā* (marriage letter), *pheras* (circumambulations), and lineage-specific rituals—yet these practices are cultural rather than scripturally mandated. Modern Jain ethics encourages mutual respect, consent, and nonviolence within marriage, and contemporary scholars highlight how Jain principles of *ahiṃsā*, *satya*, and *aparigraha* shape family life. Marriage is thus understood as a context for practicing lay virtues, supporting one another’s ethical commitments, and maintaining social harmony while acknowledging that ultimate liberation requires detachment from all worldly bonds.

primary_sources.title: Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Samantabhadra (Digambara)
primary_sources.original_text: गृहस्थस्य व्रतानि पञ्च, ब्रह्मचर्यं च यथाशक्ति।
primary_sources.transliteration: gṛhasthasya vratāni pañca, brahmacaryaṃ ca yathāśakti.
primary_sources.translation: “A householder observes five vows, and practices celibacy according to his capacity.”
primary_sources.notes: Although not a marriage manual, this text outlines the ethical framework for laypeople, including sexual restraint and fidelity. It provides the normative context in which marriage is understood.

primary_sources.title: Niśītha Cūrṇi (Śvetāmbara)
primary_sources.author: Traditional Śvetāmbara redactors
primary_sources.original_text: कम्मेहिं बंधणं लोए, गारहेसि बहु बंधणं।
primary_sources.transliteration: kammehiṃ bandhaṇaṃ loe, gārahesi bahu bandhaṇaṃ.
primary_sources.translation: “In the world, actions bind; for householders, many bonds arise.”
primary_sources.notes: This passage highlights that household life—including marriage—creates karmic entanglements. It is often cited to explain why marriage is not a path to liberation.

primary_sources.title: Sūtrakṛtāṅga Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Attributed to Mahāvīra’s disciples
primary_sources.original_text: जे ण गारहेसि बंधं, तं मुणी ण करंति।
primary_sources.transliteration: je ṇa gārahesi bandhaṃ, taṃ muṇī ṇa karanti.
primary_sources.translation: “What binds the householder, the monk does not do.”
primary_sources.notes: This contrast between monastic and lay life clarifies that marriage belongs to the domain of householders and is not part of monastic or liberation-oriented practice.

misconceptions.reality: No Jain text mandates marriage. It is a social choice within lay life, not a religious obligation.

misconceptions.myth: Marriage is a spiritual sacrament in Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: Jainism treats marriage as a worldly institution. Spiritual progress depends on ethical conduct and detachment, not marital status.

misconceptions.myth: Jain scriptures prescribe detailed marriage rituals.
misconceptions.reality: Rituals vary by community and region and are cultural, not scripturally mandated.
